title: Should I Self-Publish or Use a Hybrid Publisher?
description: Self-publishing vs hybrid publishing on one $4.99 ebook: what each path pays you per copy, IBPA’s test for a real hybrid, and what to get in writing.
lead: If your book is mainly an ebook sold on Amazon, self-publishing will almost always pay you more per copy and leave every decision with you. A hybrid publisher earns its fee only when it does publisher work you can’t buy yourself: choosing which books to take on, getting them into stores and libraries, and selling them. Whether that’s worth paying for depends on two things: the math for your book, and whether the company calling itself “hybrid” actually meets the standard. Below, we run the numbers on one ebook and list what we’d check before signing anything.
imageAlt: Two publishing path folders on a desk: self-publishing versus hybrid publishing decision

sections.heading: What changes hands on each path
paragraphs: When you self-publish, you’re the publisher. You open the KDP account (and IngramSpark, if you want wider print distribution), you decide on ISBNs and price, and Amazon pays the royalties to you. You can hire editors, designers and formatters, but they work for you and don’t take a cut of sales.

A hybrid publisher sits between that and a traditional deal. The [Independent Book Publishers Association](https://www.ibpa-online.org/page/hybridpublisher) describes it as a publisher with an author-subsidized model: you pay toward editing, design and production, the book comes out under the publisher’s imprint and ISBNs, and in exchange you get a bigger share of sales than a traditional contract would give you. IBPA’s criteria say that share should, in most cases, be more than 50% of net on both print and digital.

The catch is that “hybrid” is only a word. Any company can call itself one. IBPA’s own [criteria document](https://www.ibpa-online.org/page/hybrid-publisher-criteria-download) says a company that doesn’t meet every criterion should call itself a self-publishing service provider, and [Jane Friedman notes](https://janefriedman.com/ibpa-updates-its-hybrid-publishing-criteria/) that IBPA doesn’t currently vet its member publishers. Nobody checks the label for you. Companies that accept every manuscript and earn mainly from author fees are often called vanity presses, whatever label they use.

bullets: Delivery cost: 2 MB × $0.15 per MB = $0.30, which KDP deducts on the 70% option.
Self-published: 70% × ($4.99 − $0.30) = $3.28 per copy, paid to you.
Hybrid at IBPA’s floor: the publisher collects that same $3.28 and pays you just over half, so about $1.64 per copy.
Traditional contract, for comparison: IBPA’s guidance says most traditional publishers now pay up to 25% of net on ebooks, or about $0.82 here.
sections.heading: The per-copy math on one $4.99 ebook
paragraphs: Here’s a worked example using Amazon’s published KDP rules as of September 2026. Assume a $4.99 ebook with a 2 MB file, sold to a buyer in the US on KDP’s 70% royalty option.

So each ebook sold under a hybrid deal at IBPA’s minimum pays you about $1.64 less than self-publishing would, on top of whatever you paid up front. To see what that means for your book, divide the hybrid’s fee by the royalty you’d earn per copy. As an illustration only, using a round number and no real company’s price: earning back a $10,000 package at $1.64 a copy takes about 6,100 ebook sales.

For a fairer comparison, take the hybrid’s fee and subtract what you’d spend hiring the same editing, design and formatting yourself. What’s left is the price of the publisher’s selection, name and distribution. On top of that, you give up the $1.64 a copy for as long as the contract runs.

Two KDP details affect this math. Amazon raised the top of the 70% price band on Amazon.com from $9.99 to $12.99 on July 7, 2026, so ebooks priced up to $12.99 can now earn 70% ([KDP list price requirements](https://kdp.amazon.com/en_US/help/topic/G200634560)). And to use the 70% option, your ebook’s list price has to be at least 20% below the list price of any physical edition on Amazon ([KDP digital pricing page](https://kdp.amazon.com/en_US/help/topic/G200634500)).

bullets: Defines a mission and vision for its publishing program
Vets submissions and turns some down
Is open about costs and about each book’s realistic prospects
Offers a negotiable contract in plain language, with a rights-reversion clause
Publishes under its own imprints and ISBNs
Publishes to industry standards
Assigns real editing, design and production work

Distributes beyond uploading files to online retailers

Pays a higher-than-standard royalty
sections.heading: What a real hybrid has to do
paragraphs: If the math still points to a hybrid, check the company against IBPA’s 11 criteria. They make a good list to hand a salesperson. Ask for evidence on each line. A reputable hybrid:

Distribution deserves the hardest look. Any author can list an ebook on Amazon through KDP. IBPA asks a hybrid for a strategy that goes beyond uploading files, such as a distributor whose sales reps pitch bookstores and libraries. Ask which of their recent titles are on store shelves, and which stores.

sections.heading: When a hybrid can make sense
paragraphs: A reputable hybrid can be worth the money if you want your print book in bookstores, you’ve confirmed the company is selective and has sold books like yours, and you’ve run the math above and accept the trade. It rarely makes sense when Amazon ebooks are your main channel or when the company accepted your manuscript without asking for a single change. The same goes if you can’t get the fees, the royalty basis (net or list) and the exit terms in writing.

Jane Friedman has also warned about a bait-and-switch: a press that sounds traditional declines your book, then offers you its paid program instead. If that happens, slow down. The Alliance of Independent Authors keeps a public [watchdog rating of self-publishing services](https://selfpublishingadvice.org/best-self-publishing-services/) that’s worth checking before any sales call.

Before you pay anyone, get five things on paper: who’s named as publisher on the ISBN and copyright page, every fee with its due date and the deliverable it pays for, the royalty rate for each format and whether it’s a share of net or list, what happens to rights, files and unsold copies when the contract ends, and the rights-reversion clause itself. Our [ghostwriter contract checklist](/blog/ghostwriter-contract-checklist-nda-and-rights) is written for writing contracts, but the same questions apply here.

sections.heading: FAQ
paragraphs: ### Is hybrid publishing the same as vanity publishing?

No — a real hybrid is selective, applies editorial standards, provides genuine distribution, and reports sales transparently (the IBPA criteria). A vanity press accepts everyone, charges for production, and sells little beyond the printing itself.
### Who keeps the rights in hybrid publishing?

It depends entirely on the contract: a fair hybrid licenses limited rights for a defined term with clear reversion language. Self-publishing keeps every right with you by default — which is the baseline any hybrid offer must beat.
### Which pays more per copy, self-publishing or hybrid?

On a typical $4.99 ebook, self-publishing through KDP’s 70% plan pays you more per copy than most hybrid royalty splits after fees. A hybrid has to win on reach and services, because it rarely wins on per-copy math.
### How much does hybrid publishing cost upfront?

Packages commonly run from several thousand to tens of thousands of dollars. Before signing, price the same deliverables — editing, cover, formatting, publishing setup — bought à la carte, and compare what each dollar actually purchases.

title: How to Prepare for a Ghostwriter Discovery Call
description: What to send before a ghostwriter discovery call, what to settle in 30 minutes, and what should arrive afterward. Includes a one-page brief you can copy.
keywords: how to prepare for a ghostwriter call
lead: Our discovery calls are free and last 30 minutes. That’s enough time to decide whether we’re right for your book, as long as you send a one-page brief first. Three answers are enough to start: who the book is for, what you want it to do for you, and roughly how much time you can give it each week. Below is what to prepare, what we try to settle on the call, and what should land in your inbox afterward, whether you’re talking to us or to any other ghostwriter.

sections.heading: Send one page before the call
paragraphs: The most useful thing you can do is send a short brief a day or two ahead, so the whole 30 minutes can go to your book. Copy this, fill in what you can, and write “not sure yet” wherever you need to:

Keep confidential material out of the brief. We work under NDA on every project and send it before you share source files, so your draft manuscript, client data or private family papers can wait until it’s signed.

sections.heading: What we try to settle in 30 minutes
paragraphs: First, the job the book has to do. A 15,000-word guide that brings in consulting leads and a 50,000-word memoir for your grandchildren need different structures, interview plans and packages. So we ask about the reader and the goal before anything else.

Second, how much material already exists and how much has to come out of interviews. Our [packages](/pricing) run from up to 15,000 words to up to 100,000, and each timeline assumes a defined brief and a typical interview load. Short nonfiction often takes only a few hours of your time across the whole project. Memoirs and interview-heavy books take more, and we’ll tell you how much before you commit.
Third, whether we can staff it. We match writers by category. If we don’t have the right specialist for your subject, we’ll tell you on the call.
Fourth, what happens next. By the end of the call, you should know whether we’ll quote a standard package or a custom scope, and what we still need from you.

sections.heading: Gather material that fits your kind of book
paragraphs: For a business or expert book, the best raw material is usually what you already say out loud: recorded talks, webinar slides, podcast interviews, the email you send every new client. It shows a writer how you explain things and which examples you reach for. It also helps to name two or three books your readers already buy, with a line on what you like or dislike about each.

For a memoir, bring a rough timeline of the years the book covers, a list of the people who’ll appear in it, and a note on which letters, journals, photos or recordings you’d share once the NDA is signed. Flag anyone who’s still living and might object to how they’re portrayed, because that changes how some scenes get written.
If you have almost nothing written, that’s normal. A list of the ten stories you always end up telling is enough to start with.

bullets: Who owns the copyright, and when does it transfer?

sections.heading: FAQ
paragraphs: ### How long does a ghostwriter discovery call take?

About thirty minutes when both sides prepare: enough to settle the book’s goal, rough length, source material, timeline, and whether the fit is worth a written quote. Longer first calls usually mean the one-page brief was skipped.
### Do I need a finished outline before the discovery call?
No — a one-page brief is enough: what the book is for, who reads it, rough length, what material exists, and your deadline. The outline is part of the paid engagement, not the entry ticket.
### Is a discovery call free, and is my idea safe to share?

Reputable studios do not charge for discovery, and you only need to share the idea at a high level on the call. Detailed source material — manuscripts, transcripts, private stories — waits until an NDA is signed.
### What should I have in writing after the call?

A short written summary: scope as understood, a fixed price or a bounded estimate, a timeline band, and the named next step. A provider who resists putting those four things in an email is telling you how the project will go.
